5890.title: Possibilistic Clustering
5890.heading: Possibilistic Clustering
5890.content:
Possibilistic clustering treats membership as the degree to which an observation exemplifies each cluster and does not require memberships across clusters to sum to one. An observation can be typical of several groups or atypical of all of them.

Dropping the probability constraint makes the method more mode-seeking and can distinguish a boundary point from a remote point that is equally divided only because every option fits badly.

Privacy can support positive freedom by protecting the development and exercise of autonomous purposes. This connects data protection to the structure of personhood rather than treating it only as secrecy or control over isolated facts.

5914.heading: Positive AI Ethics
5914.content:
Positive AI ethics asks what good lives and good societies intelligent technology should help create. It complements a negative ethics focused on preventing harm, banning unacceptable uses, or complying with minimum constraints.

The question cannot be answered by technical experts or efficiency measures alone because ideas of flourishing and meaningful life are plural and politically contested. Democratic participation is needed to decide which capabilities deserve support and which forms of dependence or inequality should be avoided. Positive ethics also treats regulation as potentially enabling: rules and incentives can direct innovation toward socially valuable ends rather than merely restrict it.

5917.title: Positional Notation
5917.heading: Positional Notation
5917.content:
Positional notation is a numeral system in which a symbol's contribution depends on its location. Adjacent positions differ by a constant multiplier called the base, and each position represents a power of that base.

In base ten,

$$1234=1\cdot10^3+2\cdot10^2+3\cdot10+4.$$

The same digit therefore denotes different quantities in different positions. Positional notation makes arithmetic far more compact than a purely additive sign-value system and explains how a finite collection of digit symbols can represent arbitrarily large numbers and decimal fractions.

A positional audio component associates a [[Game Actor]] with one or more spatial sound instances. As the actor moves, the component updates the emitter position and orientation supplied to the audio engine.

The component makes spatial playback reusable across actor types and keeps transforms synchronized. It can stop owned events when removed so sounds do not outlive the world object that created them.

5926.heading: Position Velocity and Time Solution
5926.content: A position, velocity, and time solution is the joint state estimated by a satellite-navigation receiver. Pseudoranges constrain position and clock offset, while successive fixes and carrier Doppler constrain motion. Dynamic receivers often use a [[Kalman Filter]] to project position, velocity, acceleration, clock bias, and clock drift forward, then correct that prediction with new measurements. Solving these quantities together produces a continuous navigation state rather than unrelated coordinate readings.

5929.title: Pose Refinement
5929.heading: Pose Refinement
5929.content:
Pose refinement improves an initial camera-pose estimate by adjusting its parameters to reduce disagreement between observed image points and the projections predicted by the model. Reprojection error provides a measurable objective for the adjustment.

The initial closed-form estimate places the optimization near a useful solution, while iterative refinement accounts for noisy corner or feature locations. The final accuracy still depends on calibration and the geometric distribution of correspondences.

5935.title: Population Parameter
5935.heading: Population Parameter
5935.content:
A population parameter is a fixed numerical property of the population about which an analysis seeks information, such as a population mean, variance, or difference between group means. It is conceptually fixed even though it is usually unknown.

A sample supplies a [[Point Estimate]] of the parameter. Repeated sampling changes the estimate rather than the parameter, which is why uncertainty is described through a sampling distribution and interval estimate.

5938.title: Popularity Prediction
5938.heading: Popularity Prediction
5938.content:
Popularity prediction estimates the future attention received by a post, story, topic, or event. Models can use content features, early user behavior, lifecycle patterns, and the topology through which information travels.

The output may be a ranking, a class, or a numerical count. Its usefulness depends on timely forecasts and evaluation against later observations rather than fit to the training history alone.

5944.title: Polynomial
5944.heading: Polynomial
5944.content:
A polynomial is an algebraic expression formed from constants and variables raised to nonnegative integer powers, combined through addition, subtraction, and multiplication. In one variable it can be arranged as

$$a_nx^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_1x+a_0.$$

Its components are terms, and its highest nonzero exponent determines the [[Polynomial Degree]]. Polynomials can be expanded, combined, multiplied, divided with a possible remainder, and rewritten through [[Polynomial Factorization]]. Negative powers or variable denominators instead produce a [[Rational Expression]].

The source treats a polynomial as a formal coefficient sequence over a ring, not merely as an expression or the function obtained by substitution. This distinction matters over finite rings, where different formal polynomials can define the same polynomial function.

5947.title: Polynomial Time Complexity
5947.heading: Polynomial Time Complexity
5947.content:
Polynomial time complexity has the form $O(n^k)$ for some constant exponent $k$. These algorithms are generally considered tractable because their growth, although sometimes steep, remains far below [[Exponential Time Complexity]] for large inputs.

Finding a polynomial-time solution is often a practical success. Selection sort's quadratic $O(n^2)$ behavior is polynomial, though faster loglinear sorting algorithms make it unattractive for very large collections.

5953.title: Polynomial Ring
5953.heading: Polynomial Ring
5953.content:
A polynomial ring K[x₁,…,xₙ] consists of finite sums of monomials whose coefficients lie in a base ring or [[Field]]. Addition combines coefficients and multiplication uses the exponent laws, making the collection a [[Commutative Ring]].

When the coefficients form a field, the polynomial ring is an [[Integral Domain]]. Its ideals encode systems of polynomial equations and can be studied computationally through a [[Gröbner Basis]].

For a one-variable polynomial ring A[x], the source defines coefficientwise addition and convolution-style multiplication, then proves the ring properties inherited from A. When A is an integral domain, degrees of nonzero products add and A[x] is also a domain.

5956.title: Polynomial Resultant
5956.heading: Polynomial Resultant
5956.content:
The resultant of two positive-degree polynomials is the determinant of their [[Sylvester Matrix]]. It is a polynomial expression in their coefficients and vanishes exactly when the polynomials have a common factor.

The resultant can also be expressed as Af + Bg for suitable polynomials A and B. It eliminates one variable and is therefore useful in implicitization and solving polynomial systems.

5959.title: Polynomial Multiplication
5959.heading: Polynomial Multiplication
5959.content:
Polynomial multiplication distributes every term of one polynomial across every term of the other. Coefficients multiply, powers with a common base combine through the [[Laws of Exponents]], and like terms are collected after all products are formed.

The method works for any number of terms. For two binomials, the [[FOIL Method]] is a mnemonic for the same complete distribution. An omitted cross-product changes the result, which is why ((a+b)^2) equals (a^2+2ab+b^2) rather than (a^2+b^2).

5962.sourceSearchName: polynomial long division polynomial long division
5962.title: Polynomial Long Division
5962.heading: Polynomial Long Division
5962.content:
Polynomial long division divides a polynomial by a multi-term polynomial through repeated leading-term cancellation. Arrange both expressions by descending exponent, divide the leading dividend term by the leading divisor term, place that result in the quotient, multiply it by the divisor, subtract, and repeat.

The process ends when the remainder has lower [[Polynomial Degree]] than the divisor. The result has the form

$$\text{dividend}=(\text{divisor})(\text{quotient})+\text{remainder}.$$

Missing powers should be treated as zero-coefficient placeholders so columns remain aligned.

5971.title: Polynomial Interpolation
5971.heading: Polynomial Interpolation
5971.content:
Polynomial interpolation constructs a polynomial that passes through given data points. For $n+1$ distinct input values, there is a unique [[Interpolating Polynomial]] of degree at most $n$.

[[Lagrange Interpolation]] and [[Newton Divided Difference Interpolation]] express the same polynomial in different forms. Numerical behavior can deteriorate at high degree or with poorly placed nodes.

5974.title: Polynomial Implicitization
5974.heading: Polynomial Implicitization
5974.content:
Polynomial implicitization converts a polynomial parametrization xᵢ = fᵢ(t₁,…,tₘ) into equations in the x-coordinates that define the [[Zariski Closure]] of its image.

One forms an ideal generated by xᵢ − fᵢ and eliminates the parameter variables. The resulting [[Elimination Ideal]] contains exactly the implicit polynomial relations satisfied by every parametrized point.

5977.title: Polynomial Factorization
5977.heading: Polynomial Factorization
5977.content:
Polynomial factorization rewrites a polynomial as a product of simpler [[Factor]]s. It is the reverse of [[Polynomial Expansion]]:

$$ab+ac=a(b+c).$$

Methods include removing a common factor, grouping terms to expose a repeated factor, recognizing a special identity, and factoring a quadratic trinomial. A complete factorization applies methods repeatedly until the remaining factors cannot be decomposed further over the chosen number system. Multiplying the factors verifies that the original polynomial is recovered.

The modern-algebra treatment makes the coefficient field explicit because a polynomial may be reducible over one field and irreducible over another. Complete factorization is therefore always relative to the selected ring or field.

5980.title: Polynomial Expansion
5980.heading: Polynomial Expansion
5980.content:
Polynomial expansion removes products and grouping symbols by applying the [[Distributive Property]]. Every term in one factor multiplies every term in the other factors, after which [[Like Terms]] are combined.

For example,

$$(2x+3)(5x+7)=10x^2+14x+15x+21=10x^2+29x+21.$$

Expansion and [[Polynomial Factorization]] are reverse views of the same equality. Expansion exposes coefficients and like terms, while factorization exposes multiplicative structure and possible zeros.

5983.title: Polynomial Division Algorithm
5983.heading: Polynomial Division Algorithm
5983.content:
For a nonzero polynomial f over a [[Field]], every polynomial h can be written uniquely as h = fq + r, where r is zero or has smaller [[Polynomial Degree]] than f.

The algorithm repeatedly cancels the leading term of the current dividend. It proves that every ideal in a one-variable [[Polynomial Ring]] is principal and underlies the construction of Bézout identities.

The book states the algorithm over a coefficient field and uses it repeatedly: to prove the factor theorem, to reduce expressions in a simple extension, and to show that ideals of K[x] are principal.

5986.title: Polynomial Degree
5986.heading: Polynomial Degree
5986.content:
The degree of a nonzero one-variable [[Polynomial]] is the greatest exponent with a nonzero coefficient after like terms have been combined. In (3x^4-2x^3+5), the degree is four.

Degree organizes polynomial terms and controls division. [[Polynomial Long Division]] begins with the highest-degree terms and stops when the remainder has lower degree than the divisor. Multiplying nonzero polynomials adds their degrees, which helps check whether an expansion or factorization has the expected leading structure.

Over a coefficient [[Field]], the same degree comparison underlies the [[Polynomial Division Algorithm]]: a dividend has a unique quotient and a remainder whose degree is smaller than the divisor's. The degree also identifies the [[Leading Coefficient]] and controls the size of a [[Sylvester Matrix]].

The source uses degree to bound the number of roots over an integral domain and to control quotient and remainder uniqueness over a field. These results connect formal polynomial arithmetic to factorization and extension-field dimension.

6001.heading: Polar, Cylindrical, and Spherical Coordinates
6001.content: Polar coordinates locate a planar point by radius and angle. Cylindrical coordinates add height, while spherical coordinates use a radius and two angles to locate a point in three dimensions. Converting these descriptions to Cartesian components makes chart geometry, Earth locations, and the vector operations in [[Navigation Vectors and Ground Velocity]] easier to compute.

6004.content: The polar stereographic projection maps the globe to a plane tangent at a pole from a projection point at the opposite pole. Parallels become concentric circles and meridians radiate as straight lines. It is conformal and makes great-circle routes nearly straight near the pole, while scale increases as the chart extends toward lower latitudes.

6007.title: Polar Form of a Complex Number
6007.heading: Polar Form of a Complex Number
6007.content:
The polar form of a nonzero complex number is $z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$, where $r=|z|$ and $\theta$ is an argument giving its direction.

This form turns multiplication into multiplication of moduli and addition of arguments. Powers and roots therefore become simpler than in rectangular form.

6010.title: Poisson Distribution
6010.heading: Poisson Distribution
6010.content:
The Poisson distribution models a nonnegative event count through a rate parameter. Its mean and variance both equal that rate under the basic model, connecting the expected count to its sampling variability.

The source uses it for rare lottery wins, genome palindrome counts, and RNA-sequencing molecule counts. Biological variability can produce more dispersion than the basic model permits, so replication and model checking remain important.

6013.title: Pointer
6013.heading: Pointer
6013.content:
A pointer is a stored memory address that identifies another location in computer memory. Following the address gives access to the value or structure kept at that location.

In a [[Linked List]], each node contains a pointer to the next node, allowing a sequence to be formed even when nodes are stored apart. The final pointer is null, signaling that traversal has reached the end rather than another item.

6016.heading: Point-to-Point Network Topology
6016.content:
A point-to-point network topology consists of one logical connection between two nodes. It is the smallest complete network and gives each endpoint a direct path to the other.

The arrangement has low implementation and routing complexity, but it does not by itself provide an alternate route. Losing its one link removes communication between the two nodes.

Point-to-point messaging addresses a message to a particular receiver or set of intended receivers. It is suitable when one known participant should perform the work rather than every subscriber interested in a topic.

The queue or messaging system still needs access controls and delivery rules. [[Broadcast Message|Broadcast messaging]] uses the contrasting pattern in which interested receivers subscribe to a common topic or event.

6025.content:
A point marks a location without length, a line connects locations along a straight one-dimensional path, and a curve generalizes that path by allowing its direction to vary. Endpoints and intersections create the vertices through which these entities connect.

In a model, the hierarchy is operational as well as descriptive. Points can receive concentrated conditions, lines can carry one-dimensional physics or bound faces, and curves can represent edges whose continuity and curvature affect meshing.

6028.title: Point-in-Sphere Test
6028.heading: Point-in-Sphere Test
6028.content:
A point-in-sphere test subtracts the sphere center from the point and compares the squared vector length with the squared radius. The point is inside or on the sphere when the distance does not exceed the radius.

Using squared values avoids a square root. The test is a basic building block for broader [[Bounding Sphere]] intersection and containment queries.

6031.sourceSearchName: point in aabb test point in aabb test
6031.title: Point-in-AABB Test
6031.heading: Point-in-AABB Test
6031.content:
A point-in-AABB test checks whether each point coordinate lies between the corresponding minimum and maximum values of an [[Axis-Aligned Bounding Box]]. The point is contained only when all axis intervals contain it.

The test requires no square roots or rotations and is therefore inexpensive. Inclusive comparisons treat points on the boundary as contained, which is usually desirable for collision queries.

6034.title: Point Specification
6034.heading: Point Specification
6034.content:
Point specification records a three-dimensional location as the basic input to an AR model. A tracked pointer, ray, image observation, or intersection with known geometry can supply the location in the model's coordinate system.

Individual points can mark landmarks, vertices, or measurements and can be combined to infer lines, planes, and volumes. Tracking and pointing error directly limit the precision of the resulting geometry.

6037.content: A point space-time XT plot assigns each monitoring location a column, places time on the vertical axis, and maps its observed value to color. It gives a compact history of the full station network and exposes persistent high or low stations as vertical bands. Geographic position is lost because columns follow an identifier order, so [[Space-Time Point Small Multiples]] are needed to locate those patterns on a map.

Superposition reveals network-wide timing and the range of station behavior, especially when thin transparent lines soften overplotting. The view does not preserve geographic proximity and individual paths may be hard to identify. It therefore complements [[Point Space-Time XT Plot|XT plots]] and map slices rather than replacing them.

Point of view is therefore more than camera position. Choosing abstraction, detail, voice, scale, and omitted information determines whose understanding becomes normal inside the game.

6046.heading: Point of Safe Return
6046.content: The point of safe return is the farthest point an aircraft can reach outbound and still return to its departure point with the planned usable endurance. Groundspeeds differ on the outbound and inbound legs when wind is present, and reserve, contingency, alternate, and ground fuel are excluded before safe endurance is computed. Stronger wind reduces the reachable PSR distance even when it shortens one of the two legs.

6049.title: Point Space-Time Grid
6049.heading: Point Space-Time Grid
6049.content: A point space-time grid pairs a fixed set of point locations with a set of observation times. When every combination is represented, it is a [[Full Space-Time Grid]] and can be stored as an [[STFDF Object]]. With $n$ stations and $m$ times, the values must follow the object's expected $n m$ ordering. The regular structure supports directly comparable map slices and station series.

6052.title: Point Light
6052.heading: Point Light
6052.content:
A point light emits illumination outward from a particular location in the world. The direction to the light therefore changes from one surface point to another, and its contribution can weaken with distance.

Real-time shading compares the light direction with a surface normal and view direction through a reflection model such as the [[Phong Reflection Model]].

6055.title: Point Estimate
6055.heading: Point Estimate
6055.content:
A point estimate is a single value calculated from sample data to approximate an unknown [[Population Parameter]]. A sample mean estimates a population mean, and a difference between sample means estimates a population difference.

The value alone does not communicate how much it would vary across repeated samples. Pairing it with a [[Standard Error]] or [[Confidence Interval]] makes the uncertainty around the estimate visible.

6058.sourceSearchName: poincare half space model poincare half space model
6058.title: Poincare Half-Space Model
6058.heading: Poincare Half-Space Model
6058.content:
The Poincare half-space model represents hyperbolic points above a Euclidean boundary using one positive coordinate and the remaining ordinary coordinates. Its shortest paths appear as vertical lines or semicircles perpendicular to the boundary.

It is isometric to other models of [[Hyperbolic Space]], so a transformation can change the representation while preserving hyperbolic distances and geometric relationships.

6060.title: Poincare Disk Model
6060.heading: Document

6061.sourceSearchName: poincare disk model poincare disk model
6061.title: Poincare Disk Model
6061.heading: Poincare Disk Model
6061.content:
The Poincare disk model represents the infinite hyperbolic plane inside a finite Euclidean unit disk. Its boundary is infinitely far away in hyperbolic distance, and its geodesics are disk diameters or circular arcs perpendicular to that boundary.

The model supports focus-plus-context visualization because regions near the center appear large while increasingly more space is compressed near the edge. Network nodes can be assigned radial and angular coordinates inside the disk.

6064.title: PLY Polygon Format
6064.heading: PLY Polygon Format
6064.content:
PLY is a polygon file format associated with captured and scanned 3D data. A header declares the elements and properties that follow, after which vertex records and face records describe the model.

Faces index the vertex list and can contain a varying number of points rather than requiring every surface to be triangulated. In the minimal form examined by the source, PLY does not carry normals or texture coordinates. Its explicit header and simple data sections make the file's schema visible to programs that read it.

6067.heading: Pluralistic Computational Thinking Education
6067.content:
A pluralistic approach to computational thinking education accepts multiple entry points: programming, data, machines, design, simulation, and social consequences. Different learners and domains can emphasize different practices while remaining connected to computation.

Pluralism should not erase disciplinary precision. Activities need clear links to representations, machine realization, evidence, and the contexts in which a computational method is useful.

6070.title: Pluripotency
6070.heading: Pluripotency
6070.content:
Pluripotency is the capacity of a stem cell to differentiate into many cell types of the body. The property provides a flexible starting material for biofabrication when the desired mature cell is difficult to harvest or expand directly.

Pluripotency is potential, not finished function; a controlled sequence of biochemical and physical cues must guide maturation into the target lineage.

6073.sourceSearchName: plot export device plot export device
6073.title: Plot Export Device
6073.heading: Plot Export Device
6073.content:
A plot export device writes an R graphic to a file format such as PNG, PDF, or SVG with specified dimensions and resolution. Explicit export settings make the result more reproducible than manually copying a display pane.

The chosen device should suit its destination: raster output for pixel-based use and vector output for scalable lines and text.

6074.sourceSearchName: plot export device plot export device
6074.title: Plot Export Device
6074.heading: References

6076.title: Plot Matrix
6076.heading: Plot Matrix
6076.content:
A plot matrix arranges several related graphs in a common grid. It lets analysts compare transformations, variables, or stratifications without switching between separate windows and can expose patterns that only become clear side by side.

Shared ranges and consistent encodings improve comparison. Titles, legends, and text often need to be scaled or wrapped for the smaller panels so the combined figure remains legible rather than becoming a compressed collection of full-size plots.

6079.title: Plot Legend
6079.heading: Plot Legend
6079.content:
A plot legend maps visual encodings such as color, symbol, fill, or line type to substantive categories. Its ordering must match the ordering used to draw the data, or the graph will communicate the wrong group identities.

Placement and scale should preserve the data region. When several lines are overlaid, the legend should repeat the same widths, colors, and line types used in the plot rather than rely on a separate default style.

6082.title: Plot Encoding
6082.heading: Plot Encoding
6082.content:
Plot encoding assigns data meaning to position, length, color, symbol, fill, or line type. Position on a common axis is generally easier to compare precisely than angle or area, while redundant encodings can make groups distinguishable in grayscale or for color-impaired readers.

An encoding should remain consistent between the main graph and its [[Plot Legend]]. Decorative variation that has no data meaning can create false groupings or distract from the comparison the figure is meant to support.

6084.sourceSearchName: plot axis scaling plot axis scaling
6084.title: Plot Axis Scaling
6084.heading: Document

6085.sourceSearchName: plot axis scaling plot axis scaling
6085.title: Plot Axis Scaling
6085.heading: Plot Axis Scaling
6085.content:
Plot axis scaling selects the displayed range, tick marks, and label format for a graph. A focused range can reveal small but meaningful differences, as when survival probabilities all remain near one, while a broad range provides context about absolute magnitude.

Scaling must not conceal relevant observations or exaggerate an effect. Analysts should derive plausible limits from descriptive statistics, label the units, and avoid formats such as unnecessary scientific notation when they impede interpretation.

6088.title: Playtest Evidence Review
6088.heading: Playtest Evidence Review
6088.content:
A playtest evidence review organizes observed strengths, breakdowns, comments, behaviors, bugs, and emergent ideas before the team chooses revisions. It looks for recurring patterns while preserving important outliers relevant to the design question.

The review compares outcomes with [[Design Values]] rather than with an undefined notion of improvement. A surprising behavior may be a defect, a new possibility, or irrelevant depending on the experience the game is meant to create.

6090.title: Playtesting
6090.heading: Document
6090.content:
2026-09-05 14:36

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Design Methods]] [[Game Production Planning and Milestones]] [[Agile Engineering and Quality]] [[Iterative Game Design Cycle]] [[Game Playtesting Practice]]

6091.title: Playtesting
6091.heading: Playtesting
6091.content:
Playtesting observes other people interacting with a game to evaluate the experience rather than to find code defects. It reveals whether players form workable mental models, understand their goals, make meaningful decisions, and remain engaged.

Tests should begin early, use clear questions and appropriate participants, and avoid coaching or defending the design. Observations, concise surveys, and player comments identify problems; the designer analyzes recurring evidence and decides how to solve them.

Playtesting and iteration also reveal whether a game's expressive conversation produces the intended response. That response need not be conventional fun; the test can examine whether the designed system communicates a serious, difficult, or reflective experience clearly.

Agile teams involve players throughout development rather than waiting for a separate final phase. Informal sessions and more controlled studies reinforce the [[Definition of Done]], uncover usability and challenge problems, and give the Product Backlog evidence; they should not be expected to invent the game's breakthrough concept for the team.

6094.title: Playtest Plan
6094.heading: Playtest Plan
6094.content:
A playtest plan specifies the design question, suitable prototype and participants, time and place, facilitator procedure, and method of recording evidence. It prevents the session from becoming unstructured play whose results cannot be interpreted.

Planning also identifies what not to explain, which behaviors to observe, and how discussion will follow play. The plan should be narrow enough that the team knows what the session can and cannot establish.

6097.title: Player-Killing
6097.heading: Player-Killing
6097.content:
Player-killing is nonconsensual combat in an online world, often involving a stronger participant attacking a weaker one for possessions or harassment. It differs from mutually accepted competitive play.

The design must decide where combat is allowed, how consent works, what can be lost, and what protection or redress exists. Unrestricted player-killing can drive away new or noncompetitive players.

6099.heading: Document

6100.sourceSearchName: player controlled difficulty player controlled difficulty
6100.title: Player-Controlled Difficulty
6100.heading: Player-Controlled Difficulty
6100.content:
Player-controlled difficulty lets players alter the resistance they encounter through choices made inside play. A player might advance into a more dangerous area, retreat to safer space, accept an optional power, or choose when to approach a difficult challenge.

Unlike a fixed [[Difficulty Mode]] selected before the system is understood, these decisions can be grounded in experience. They make pacing part of the player's performance while preserving concrete rules and consequences.

6103.sourceSearchName: player centric game design player centric game design
6103.title: Player-Centric Game Design
6103.heading: Player-Centric Game Design
6103.content:
Player-centric game design evaluates decisions through the experience of a representative member of the intended audience. The designer asks whether each feature entertains and serves that player rather than favoring the team's convenience or personal preferences.

The approach begins only after the target audience is defined. It is not a claim that every possible player must be satisfied, but a discipline for keeping the chosen player visible throughout development.

6105.heading: Document

6106.sourceSearchName: player based balancing player based balancing
6106.title: Player-Based Balancing
6106.heading: Player-Based Balancing
6106.content:
Player-based balancing uses observed play and player reports to revise a game's balance. It closes the [[Designer Loop]] by comparing the intended experience with what players actually understand, choose, and feel.

Players are strong evidence about the problems they experience but are not necessarily reliable designers of solutions. The designer interprets their feedback alongside behavior and the game's systemic goals.

6108.heading: Document
6108.content:

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Character and Interactive Story Design]]

6109.sourceSearchName: player avatar relationship player avatar relationship
6109.title: Player-Avatar Relationship
6109.heading: Player-Avatar Relationship
6109.content:
The player-avatar relationship is the psychological and mechanical connection between a player and the character representing them. A blank or customizable avatar encourages projection, while a strongly authored protagonist asks the player to guide a distinct personality.

The relationship should match the game's story and control. Forcing choices that contradict an established character or withholding actions implied by the role can make the player feel detached from both avatar and plot.

6110.sourceSearchName: player avatar relationship player avatar relationship
6110.title: Player-Avatar Relationship
6110.heading: References

6112.title: Player Role
6112.heading: Player Role
6112.content:
The player role describes who or what the player is within the game and what activities that position permits. It might be one avatar, a party leader, a manager, a vehicle operator, or a shifting set of responsibilities.

Clarifying the role helps explain goals, actions, rules, and perspective. If the role changes, the game must communicate why it changed and how the player should adapt.

6115.title: Player Retention
6115.heading: Player Retention
6115.content:
Player retention is the proportion of players who return after their first experience, commonly observed at later day-based checkpoints. It indicates whether the game continues to offer understandable goals and reasons to reengage.

Retention is interpreted through [[Cohort Analysis]] because day-to-day totals alone mix players at different stages. Weak early retention can point to problems in the [[First-Time User Experience]], balance, or the enduring core loop.

6118.title: Player Performance
6118.heading: Player Performance
6118.content:
Player performance is the particular way a player realizes a designed [[Game Scene]] through timing, movement, strategy, and choice. The designer shapes the scene and provides its vocabulary, but the player determines the exact performance.

Meaningful performance requires enough liberty for individual decisions to matter. At the same time, choices remain bounded by available [[Game Verb|verbs]] and rules, allowing a scene to have a recognizable shape without prescribing every action.

6121.title: Player Motivation
6121.heading: Player Motivation
6121.content:
Player motivation is the pattern of desired activity and reward that draws a person into play. The source groups recurring motivations as action, social connection, mastery, achievement, immersion, and creativity, with players often combining several.

Motivations guide the [[Target Audience]] description and the interaction loops a game emphasizes. They are more useful than a generic assumption that all players want the same form of fun.

6124.title: Player Mental Model
6124.heading: Player Mental Model
6124.content:
A player mental model is the player's evolving understanding of the game's state, rules, goals, and likely outcomes. It includes remembered decisions, predictions, learned skills, and both explicit and self-created goals.

The player tests this model through action and revises it from [[Feedback]]. A coherent relationship with the [[Game Model]] enables planning and mastery, while effects that seem arbitrary or incomprehensible weaken engagement.

6127.title: Player Goal
6127.heading: Player Goal
6127.content:
A player goal is a desired state that organizes attention and action during play. Goals can operate over immediate, short-term, and long-term timescales and may be supplied explicitly by the game or created by the player.

Goals give consequences meaning and allow [[Feedback]] to be interpreted as progress, setback, or new opportunity. Nested goals connect moment-to-moment [[Core Gameplay Loop|core loops]] to broader [[Progression System|progression]].

A goal may be explicit, implied by the system's rewards and resistance, selected from many authored objectives, or invented by the player inside an open system. Increasing player control over purpose widens the conversation but does not remove the boundaries established by the rules.

6130.title: Player Expression
6130.heading: Player Expression
6130.content:
Player expression is the communication of preference, style, intention, or identity through choices made in play. It can appear in movement, strategy, character presentation, cooperation, aggression, restraint, or goals the player invents.

Expression does not require unlimited freedom. A focused set of [[Game Verb|verbs]] can support distinctive performances when their relationships create several meaningful ways to proceed.

6133.title: Player Action
6133.heading: Player Action
6133.content:
A player action is a behavior permitted by the game's rules. Many actions are tools for overcoming challenges, while others support exploration, expression, communication, experimentation, or simple pleasure.

The action set defines what the player can actually do, not merely what the fiction claims is possible. A small group of reusable actions can support many challenges when their consequences combine consistently.

6136.title: Player Disconnection
6136.heading: Player Disconnection
6136.content:
Player disconnection occurs when a participant leaves or loses network contact during an online session. The game may not be able to distinguish a deliberate exit from equipment or connection failure.

Possible responses include forfeiture, pausing, replacement by an automated player, reconnection windows, or continuing with fewer participants. The rule must protect the remaining players without punishing unavoidable failure excessively.

6139.title: Playable Game Prototype
6139.heading: Playable Game Prototype
6139.content:
A playable game prototype is an early functional artifact that lets a person perform the game's main actions. It can omit final goals, content, visuals, and sound when those elements are not necessary to test the core interaction.

Its roughness is deliberate. The prototype asks whether the basic activity produces useful feedback and possibilities before the team invests in making that activity look complete.

6142.title: Play
6142.heading: Play
6142.content:
Play is a nonessential human activity usually undertaken voluntarily and often for recreation. It can be structured or unstructured, solitary or social, and it does not require a formal victory condition.

A [[Game]] is one organized form of play. It adds a pretended context, at least one arbitrary and nontrivial goal, and rules that constrain how participants pursue that goal.
